name.text: The three layers bottom to top

questiontext.text: In the classic test automation pyramid (Mike Cohn), the layers from bottom to top are:

answer.text: Unit tests (base), integration/service tests (middle), UI/end-to-end tests (top)

feedback.text: Correct — a wide base of unit tests, a narrower band of integration/service tests, and a thin top of UI/E2E tests.

answer.text: UI/end-to-end tests (base), integration tests (middle), unit tests (top)

feedback.text: That is upside down — it describes the ice-cream-cone anti-pattern, not the pyramid.

answer.text: Integration tests (base), unit tests (middle), UI tests (top)

feedback.text: Unit tests form the base, not the middle.

answer.text: Unit tests (base), UI/end-to-end tests (middle), integration tests (top)

feedback.text: UI/E2E sits at the top and integration in the middle, not the other way round.

generalfeedback.text: Bottom to top: many unit tests, fewer integration/service tests, few UI/end-to-end tests. The width of each layer suggests how many tests of that kind you should have.

questiontext.text: In a healthy test automation pyramid, which layer should contain the most tests?

answer.text: Unit tests (the base)

feedback.text: Correct — the base is the widest layer, so unit tests are the most numerous.

answer.text: UI/end-to-end tests (the top)

feedback.text: The top is the narrowest layer and should have the fewest tests.

answer.text: Integration/service tests (the middle)

feedback.text: The middle sits between the two; the base (unit) has more.

answer.text: All three layers should have equal numbers

feedback.text: A pyramid is deliberately unequal — a wide base narrowing to a thin top.

generalfeedback.text: The base is the widest part of the pyramid: unit tests are the cheapest and fastest, so you can afford the most of them.

questiontext.text: In a healthy test automation pyramid, which layer should contain the fewest tests?

answer.text: UI/end-to-end tests (the top)

feedback.text: Correct — the top is the narrowest layer, so UI/E2E tests are the fewest.

answer.text: Unit tests (the base)

feedback.text: Unit tests are the most numerous, not the fewest.

answer.text: Integration/service tests (the middle)

feedback.text: The middle has more than the top; the top (UI/E2E) is the fewest.

answer.text: They should all have the same small number

feedback.text: The layers differ; the top layer specifically is the thinnest.

generalfeedback.text: UI/end-to-end tests are slow, expensive, and brittle, so you keep only a few of them at the narrow top of the pyramid.

questiontext.text: Which set of properties best describes unit tests at the base of the pyramid?

answer.text: Fast, cheap, isolated, stable, and numerous

feedback.text: Correct — these properties are exactly why unit tests form the wide base.

answer.text: Slow, expensive, and few

feedback.text: Those are properties of UI/end-to-end tests at the top, not unit tests.

answer.text: Slow but very cheap and numerous

feedback.text: Unit tests are fast, not slow; speed is one of their defining traits.

answer.text: Realistic, end-to-end, and brittle

feedback.text: Those describe UI/E2E tests; unit tests are isolated and stable.

generalfeedback.text: Unit tests run in milliseconds, are cheap to write and maintain, are isolated from external systems, are deterministic/stable, and pinpoint failures — so you keep many of them and run them constantly.

questiontext.text: Which set of properties best describes UI/end-to-end tests at the top of the pyramid?

answer.text: Slow, expensive, brittle/flaky, few — but the most realistic

feedback.text: Correct — they exercise the whole system like a real user, which is realistic but costly and fragile.

answer.text: Fast, cheap, stable, and numerous

feedback.text: Those are unit-test properties, not UI/E2E.

answer.text: Fast and deterministic but not realistic

feedback.text: UI/E2E tests are slow and the most realistic, not fast and unrealistic.

answer.text: Cheap to maintain and rarely flaky

feedback.text: They are the most expensive to maintain and the most prone to flakiness.

generalfeedback.text: End-to-end tests drive the whole system through the UI, so they are the most realistic but also the slowest, costliest, and flakiest — you keep only a few.

questiontext.text: The middle layer of the test automation pyramid consists of:

answer.text: Integration/service (API) tests that check how components work together below the UI

feedback.text: Correct — the middle exercises component interactions and service/API boundaries without going through the UI.

answer.text: Unit tests of single isolated functions

feedback.text: Those are the base layer, not the middle.

answer.text: End-to-end tests driven through the browser UI

feedback.text: Those are the top layer, not the middle.

answer.text: Manual exploratory testing sessions

feedback.text: The pyramid describes automated test layers; the middle is integration/service tests.

generalfeedback.text: The middle band holds integration/service/API tests: moderate in speed and cost, they verify that components interact correctly at a level below the full UI.

questiontext.text: The ice-cream cone anti-pattern refers to a test distribution that is:

answer.text: Inverted — many UI/manual tests on top and too few unit tests at the bottom

feedback.text: Correct — the pyramid is turned upside down, with the bulk of testing at the slow, brittle top.

answer.text: A healthy pyramid with a wide unit base

feedback.text: That is the desired shape, not the anti-pattern.

answer.text: A fat unit base with a fat E2E top and a thin middle

feedback.text: That is the hourglass anti-pattern, not the ice-cream cone.

answer.text: Having no automated tests at all

feedback.text: The ice-cream cone still has many tests — they are just concentrated at the wrong (top) layer.

generalfeedback.text: The ice-cream cone is the inverted pyramid: most tests are slow, expensive UI or manual tests, with too small a unit base — giving slow, flaky, costly feedback.

name.text: Read a ratio to identify the layer (base)

questiontext.text: A team reports its automated tests as roughly 70% / 20% / 10% across the three pyramid layers. The 70% slice is the fastest and cheapest to run. Which layer is it?

answer.text: Unit tests (the base)

feedback.text: Correct — the largest, fastest, cheapest slice is the unit base.

answer.text: Integration/service tests (the middle)

feedback.text: The middle is the 20% slice here, not the 70%.

answer.text: UI/end-to-end tests (the top)

feedback.text: The top is the smallest, slowest slice — 10%, not 70%.

answer.text: Cannot be determined from the numbers

feedback.text: The largest, fastest, cheapest slice is unmistakably the unit base.

generalfeedback.text: In an illustrative 70/20/10 split, the 70% (largest, fastest, cheapest) is unit, 20% is integration, and 10% is UI/E2E. Treat the exact ratio as illustrative, not a law.

questiontext.text: Which layer gives the testing that is closest to a real user's experience of the whole system?

answer.text: UI/end-to-end tests (the top)

feedback.text: Correct — E2E tests drive the fully integrated system as a user would, so they are the most realistic.

answer.text: Unit tests (the base)

feedback.text: Unit tests check pieces in isolation and are the least like a real end-user scenario.

answer.text: Integration/service tests (the middle)

feedback.text: These are more realistic than unit tests but still below the full-UI, whole-system level.

answer.text: All layers are equally realistic

feedback.text: Realism increases as you move up the pyramid; the top is the most realistic.

generalfeedback.text: Realism rises as you climb the pyramid: E2E tests exercise the whole system through its real interfaces, so they most closely match actual user behaviour — at the cost of speed and stability.

name.text: Which tests run constantly to gate commits

questiontext.text: Which layer's tests are typically run on every commit to give developers fast feedback in CI?

answer.text: Unit tests (the base)

feedback.text: Correct — being fast and stable, unit tests can run constantly and gate each commit.

answer.text: UI/end-to-end tests (the top)

feedback.text: E2E tests are too slow and flaky to run on every commit; they are run less often.

answer.text: Only manual tests

feedback.text: Manual tests cannot gate every commit; fast automated unit tests do.

answer.text: No tests should run on a commit

feedback.text: Fast unit tests are exactly what should gate each commit in CI.

generalfeedback.text: Because unit tests are fast and deterministic, they run on every commit as the CI gate; slower UI/E2E tests run less frequently (e.g. nightly or before release).

questiontext.text: In the test automation pyramid, unit tests form the wide base.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — unit tests are the most numerous and sit at the base.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Unit tests do form the base; putting UI/E2E at the base is the inverted anti-pattern.

generalfeedback.text: The pyramid's wide base is unit tests — fast, cheap, and numerous — with fewer integration tests above and few UI/E2E tests at the top.

questiontext.text: In a healthy pyramid, end-to-end (UI) tests should outnumber unit tests.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: This is the inverted (ice-cream-cone) shape, not a healthy pyramid.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — unit tests should far outnumber E2E tests; the reverse is the ice-cream-cone anti-pattern.

generalfeedback.text: A healthy pyramid has many unit tests and few E2E tests. When E2E tests outnumber unit tests you have an inverted pyramid (ice-cream cone).

name.text: Layer that tests APIs below the UI

questiontext.text: Which layer verifies that components and services interact correctly through their APIs, below the UI?

answer.text: Integration/service tests (the middle)

feedback.text: Correct — the middle layer tests interactions at the service/API level, below the full UI.

answer.text: Unit tests (the base)

feedback.text: Unit tests exercise a single component in isolation, not interactions across an API.

answer.text: UI/end-to-end tests (the top)

feedback.text: E2E tests go through the UI; the middle layer deliberately tests below it.

answer.text: Acceptance sign-off meetings

feedback.text: That is not an automated test layer; API-level testing is the integration/service layer.

generalfeedback.text: Integration/service tests hit APIs and component boundaries directly, avoiding the slow, brittle UI while still checking that parts work together.

questiontext.text: Which layer's tests are typically the most brittle and flaky?

answer.text: UI/end-to-end tests (the top)

feedback.text: Correct — depending on the whole stack, timing, and the UI makes E2E tests the most fragile.

answer.text: Unit tests (the base)

feedback.text: Unit tests are isolated and deterministic, so they are the most stable, not the flakiest.

answer.text: Integration/service tests (the middle)

feedback.text: These are more fragile than unit tests but less flaky than full UI/E2E tests.

answer.text: All layers are equally flaky

feedback.text: Flakiness concentrates at the top; unit tests are the most stable.

generalfeedback.text: E2E tests depend on many integrated parts, external state, timing, and the UI, so they flake most. Flakiness is concentrated at the top of the pyramid.

name.text: Read a ratio to identify the middle

questiontext.text: A suite is split 70% / 20% / 10% across unit / integration / UI. The 20% slice corresponds to which layer?

answer.text: Integration/service tests (the middle)

feedback.text: Correct — 20% is the middle band between the 70% unit base and the 10% UI top.

answer.text: Unit tests (the base)

feedback.text: Unit is the 70% slice, not the 20%.

answer.text: UI/end-to-end tests (the top)

feedback.text: UI/E2E is the smallest slice — 10%, not 20%.

answer.text: Manual tests

feedback.text: The pyramid's automated middle band is integration/service tests.

generalfeedback.text: In an illustrative 70/20/10 split, the 20% middle is integration/service tests, between the unit base (70%) and the UI top (10%).

questiontext.text: A team's automated suite is slow to run and frequently flaky. Which layer is most likely over-weighted?

answer.text: UI/end-to-end tests (the top)

feedback.text: Correct — too many slow, brittle E2E tests produce exactly this symptom.

answer.text: Unit tests (the base)

feedback.text: Many unit tests keep the suite fast and stable, not slow and flaky.

answer.text: There is no way to tell from the symptom

feedback.text: Slow and flaky strongly points to an over-large UI/E2E top.

answer.text: The suite must have too few tests overall

feedback.text: The problem is the mix (too many E2E), not simply the total count.

generalfeedback.text: Slowness and flakiness concentrate at the top of the pyramid, so a slow, flaky suite usually means too many UI/E2E tests relative to unit and integration tests.

questiontext.text: The guideline to push tests down the pyramid means:

answer.text: Test each behaviour at the lowest layer that still gives adequate confidence

feedback.text: Correct — prefer a fast unit or integration test over an E2E test whenever it gives enough confidence.

answer.text: Delete all higher-level tests and rely only on the UI

feedback.text: Pushing down means moving coverage lower, not removing all higher tests or relying on the UI.

answer.text: Move all tests up to the end-to-end layer for realism

feedback.text: That inverts the pyramid; pushing down means the opposite.

answer.text: Run tests in a different physical location

feedback.text: "Down" refers to lower pyramid layers, not physical placement.

generalfeedback.text: Push-down means choosing the lowest (cheapest, fastest, most stable) layer that still gives adequate confidence for a given behaviour, reserving slow E2E tests for what only they can cover.

questiontext.text: Which distribution describes a healthy pyramid rather than an ice-cream cone?

answer.text: Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, few UI/E2E tests

feedback.text: Correct — a wide unit base tapering to a thin UI top is the healthy pyramid.

answer.text: Many UI/E2E tests, fewer integration tests, few unit tests

feedback.text: That is the inverted ice-cream cone, not a healthy pyramid.

answer.text: Equal numbers of unit, integration, and UI tests

feedback.text: A pyramid is deliberately unequal, widest at the unit base.

answer.text: Only UI tests and nothing else

feedback.text: That is an extreme ice-cream cone with no base at all.

generalfeedback.text: A healthy pyramid narrows as it rises: the most unit tests, fewer integration tests, and the fewest UI/E2E tests. The ice-cream cone is this shape inverted.

name.text: Why unit tests form the base

questiontext.text: Why do unit tests form the base of the pyramid?

answer.text: They are fast, cheap, stable, and pinpoint failures, so you can afford many of them and run them constantly

feedback.text: Correct — these properties make a large unit base the most efficient foundation.

answer.text: They are the most realistic, so they deserve the most coverage

feedback.text: Realism is a property of E2E tests, not unit tests; that is not why unit tests form the base.

answer.text: They are the only tests capable of finding any defects

feedback.text: Higher layers find defects unit tests cannot (e.g. interface and end-to-end faults).

answer.text: They are the slowest, so they must run first

feedback.text: Unit tests are the fastest, which is precisely why there are many of them.

generalfeedback.text: Unit tests are fast, cheap, isolated, deterministic, and localise failures precisely — so a large base of them gives quick, reliable feedback at low cost.

questiontext.text: A suite has 200 tests distributed as an illustrative 70% / 20% / 10% (unit / integration / UI). How many are unit tests?

feedback.text: Correct — 70% of 200 = 140.
40 is the integration count (20% of 200), not the unit count.
20 is the UI count (10% of 200), not the unit count.
70 is the percentage, not the number of tests; 70% of 200 is 140.

generalfeedback.text: 0.70 × 200 = 140 unit, 0.20 × 200 = 40 integration, 0.10 × 200 = 20 UI. The ratio is illustrative, not a rule.

questiontext.text: A suite has 300 tests distributed as an illustrative 70% / 20% / 10% (unit / integration / UI). How many are integration tests?

feedback.text: Correct — 20% of 300 = 60.
210 is the unit count (70% of 300), not the integration count.
30 is the UI count (10% of 300), not the integration count.
20 is the percentage, not the number; 20% of 300 is 60.

generalfeedback.text: 0.20 × 300 = 60 integration (with 210 unit and 30 UI). Treat the 70/20/10 split as illustrative.

name.text: Classify a test: full checkout flow

questiontext.text: A test opens the browser, logs in, adds an item to the cart, and completes checkout as a real user would. Which layer does it belong to?

answer.text: UI/end-to-end (the top)

feedback.text: Correct — driving the whole application through the UI as a user is an E2E test.

answer.text: Unit (the base)

feedback.text: A whole-application browser flow is far broader than a single isolated unit.

answer.text: Integration/service (the middle)

feedback.text: This goes through the UI and the full stack, which is E2E rather than a below-the-UI integration test.

answer.text: It is not a test of any pyramid layer

feedback.text: It is a classic end-to-end test at the top of the pyramid.

generalfeedback.text: Exercising the entire integrated system through the real UI, as a user would, is the definition of an end-to-end (top-layer) test.

name.text: Classify a test: one pure function

questiontext.text: A test calls a single pure function with fixed inputs and asserts its return value, with no database, network, or UI involved. Which layer does it belong to?

answer.text: Unit (the base)

feedback.text: Correct — an isolated test of one function's logic is a unit test.

answer.text: Integration/service (the middle)

feedback.text: Nothing is being integrated here; it is a single isolated function.

answer.text: UI/end-to-end (the top)

feedback.text: No UI or full-system flow is involved, so it is not E2E.

answer.text: It cannot be automated

feedback.text: A pure-function assertion is one of the easiest tests to automate — a unit test.

generalfeedback.text: Testing one function in isolation with no external dependencies is the textbook unit test at the base of the pyramid.

name.text: Classify a test: service talks to database

questiontext.text: A test starts a service and a real test database, then checks that saving and reloading a record through the service's API works correctly — without opening any UI. Which layer does it belong to?

answer.text: Integration/service (the middle)

feedback.text: Correct — it checks the service and database working together below the UI.

answer.text: Unit (the base)

feedback.text: It involves two collaborating components (service + database), so it is not an isolated unit test.

answer.text: UI/end-to-end (the top)

feedback.text: No UI is involved; the test stops at the service/API level.

answer.text: It is a performance test only

feedback.text: It checks functional correctness of an interaction, which is an integration/service test.

generalfeedback.text: Exercising a real interaction between components (service and database) through the API, without the UI, is a middle-layer integration/service test.

questiontext.text: A team relies mostly on manual and UI tests, with almost no unit tests. This distribution is called:

answer.text: An ice-cream cone (inverted pyramid)

feedback.text: Correct — most effort at the slow top and a tiny unit base is the ice-cream cone.

answer.text: A healthy pyramid

feedback.text: A healthy pyramid has a large unit base, the opposite of this.

answer.text: An hourglass

feedback.text: An hourglass has a fat unit base and fat E2E top with a thin middle; here the unit base is nearly missing.

answer.text: A well-balanced test portfolio

feedback.text: Over-relying on manual/UI tests is unbalanced and gives slow, costly feedback.

generalfeedback.text: Heavy manual/UI testing with a tiny unit base is the classic ice-cream-cone anti-pattern: the pyramid turned upside down.

questiontext.text: Across the pyramid, flakiness (non-deterministic pass/fail) is generally concentrated at:

answer.text: The top (UI/end-to-end tests)

feedback.text: Correct — dependence on the whole stack, timing, and the UI makes the top layer flakiest.

answer.text: The base (unit tests)

feedback.text: Unit tests are isolated and deterministic, so they flake least.

answer.text: Evenly across all three layers

feedback.text: Flakiness rises as you climb; it is not even.

answer.text: Only in tests that have no assertions

feedback.text: Flakiness is about non-determinism, and it concentrates in E2E tests regardless of assertions.

generalfeedback.text: The higher a test sits, the more moving parts, timing, and environment it depends on, so flakiness concentrates at the UI/E2E top.

name.text: Why fast unit tests gate every commit

questiontext.text: Why are fast unit tests the natural choice to run on every commit in CI?

answer.text: They finish quickly and are deterministic, so they give reliable feedback without slowing the pipeline

feedback.text: Correct — speed plus stability makes them ideal as a per-commit gate.

answer.text: They are the only tests that can fail

feedback.text: Any layer's tests can fail; unit tests are chosen for speed and stability.

answer.text: They exercise the whole system most realistically

feedback.text: That is E2E; unit tests are chosen precisely because they are fast, not because they are realistic.

answer.text: They never need to be maintained

feedback.text: All tests need maintenance; the reason for the gate is speed and determinism.

generalfeedback.text: A per-commit gate must be fast and reliable. Unit tests run in seconds and are deterministic, so they fit; slow, flaky E2E tests are run less often.

questiontext.text: A suite has 500 tests distributed as an illustrative 70% / 20% / 10% (unit / integration / UI). How many are UI tests?

feedback.text: Correct — 10% of 500 = 50.
350 is the unit count (70% of 500), not the UI count.
100 is the integration count (20% of 500), not the UI count.
10 is the percentage, not the number; 10% of 500 is 50.

generalfeedback.text: 0.10 × 500 = 50 UI (with 350 unit and 100 integration). The split is illustrative.

name.text: Move coverage down to fix slow flaky suite

questiontext.text: To fix a slow, flaky suite, it is generally better to move coverage down — replacing some E2E tests with equivalent unit or integration tests where they give adequate confidence.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — pushing coverage to lower layers speeds up the suite and reduces flakiness.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Moving coverage down is exactly the standard remedy for a slow, flaky suite.

generalfeedback.text: Speed and stability improve as you move down the pyramid, so replacing redundant E2E tests with lower-level tests (where confidence is adequate) is the usual fix.

name.text: Choosing the layer for a behaviour

questiontext.text: A behaviour can be verified equally well by a fast unit test or by a slow E2E test. Which should you generally prefer?

answer.text: The unit test, because it is the lowest layer that gives adequate confidence

feedback.text: Correct — push down: use the cheapest, fastest test that suffices.

answer.text: The E2E test, because higher tests are always better

feedback.text: Higher tests are slower and flakier; you do not use them when a lower one suffices.

answer.text: Both, always, for every behaviour

feedback.text: Duplicating every behaviour at E2E inflates a slow, flaky top layer needlessly.

answer.text: Neither; leave the behaviour untested

feedback.text: The behaviour should be tested — at the lowest adequate layer.

generalfeedback.text: When two layers give the same confidence, choose the lower one. Reserve E2E tests for behaviours only they can adequately cover.

questiontext.text: A suite is distributed 10% unit / 20% integration / 70% UI. This is best diagnosed as:

answer.text: An ice-cream cone — the pyramid is inverted, with far too many UI tests

feedback.text: Correct — the bulk of testing sits at the slow, brittle top with a tiny unit base.

answer.text: A healthy pyramid

feedback.text: A healthy pyramid has the most unit tests; here unit is only 10%.

answer.text: An hourglass

feedback.text: An hourglass has fat top and base with a thin middle; here the base (unit) is thin, not fat.

answer.text: A perfectly balanced portfolio

feedback.text: Concentrating 70% at the UI top is unbalanced — the ice-cream-cone anti-pattern.

generalfeedback.text: Most tests at the top and few at the base is the inverted pyramid, i.e. the ice-cream cone: slow, flaky, expensive feedback.

questiontext.text: Given an ice-cream-cone distribution (too many UI tests, too few unit tests), the standard remediation is to:

answer.text: Add unit and integration tests and push coverage down, keeping only the E2E tests that earn their place

feedback.text: Correct — rebuild the base and trim redundant E2E tests to restore the pyramid shape.

answer.text: Add even more UI tests for realism

feedback.text: That worsens the inversion; the top is already too heavy.

answer.text: Delete all UI tests entirely

feedback.text: A few E2E tests are still valuable; the fix is rebalancing, not removing the whole top.

answer.text: Stop automated testing and rely on manual testing

feedback.text: That deepens the anti-pattern rather than fixing it.

generalfeedback.text: Fix an ice-cream cone by pushing coverage down: grow the unit and integration layers and keep only the high-value E2E tests, restoring a wide base.

questiontext.text: A suite has 50% unit / 5% integration / 45% UI — a fat base and a fat top with almost nothing in between. This is best diagnosed as:

answer.text: An hourglass — the integration/service middle is too thin

feedback.text: Correct — a starved middle with heavy base and top is the hourglass anti-pattern.

answer.text: An ice-cream cone

feedback.text: An ice-cream cone is inverted with a tiny base; here the base is large.

answer.text: A healthy pyramid

feedback.text: A healthy pyramid has a substantial middle; here it is nearly missing.

answer.text: An over-tested middle layer

feedback.text: The middle is under-tested (5%), not over-tested.

generalfeedback.text: A fat unit base plus a fat E2E top with a starved integration middle is the hourglass: interaction faults slip through because the service layer is barely tested.

questiontext.text: The correct remediation for an hourglass distribution is to:

answer.text: Build up the integration/service (middle) layer and move some E2E coverage down into it

feedback.text: Correct — thickening the middle catches interaction faults faster than E2E and restores the taper.

answer.text: Add more UI tests to compensate for the thin middle

feedback.text: That relies on the slow top to catch interaction faults instead of fixing the missing middle.

answer.text: Remove unit tests so the shape looks more like a pyramid

feedback.text: You never fix a shape by discarding the fast, valuable base.

answer.text: Do nothing; an hourglass is optimal

feedback.text: An hourglass leaves interaction faults poorly covered; it is an anti-pattern to correct.

generalfeedback.text: Fix an hourglass by growing the integration/service middle — the fastest place to catch component-interaction faults — and pushing some E2E coverage down into it.

questiontext.text: Which statement best captures the core trade-off between the pyramid's layers?

answer.text: Higher layers give more realism and confidence but slower, costlier, flakier feedback; lower layers give faster, cheaper, more stable feedback with less end-to-end realism

feedback.text: Correct — this is the central speed/cost-versus-realism trade-off of the pyramid.

answer.text: Higher layers are strictly better than lower layers in every respect

feedback.text: Higher layers are slower, costlier, and flakier; they are not strictly better.

answer.text: Lower layers are more realistic than higher layers

feedback.text: Realism increases as you go up, not down.

answer.text: All layers have identical speed, cost, and realism

feedback.text: The layers differ sharply on exactly these dimensions.

generalfeedback.text: Climbing the pyramid trades speed, cost, and stability for realism and end-to-end confidence. The pyramid shape balances these by favouring many cheap low-level tests and few expensive high-level ones.

name.text: Why flakiness concentrates at the top

questiontext.text: Why does flakiness concentrate in the top layer of the pyramid?

answer.text: E2E tests depend on the whole integrated stack, timing, and external state, giving many chances for non-deterministic failures

feedback.text: Correct — more moving parts and timing dependencies mean more non-determinism.

answer.text: E2E tests have weaker assertions than unit tests

feedback.text: Flakiness comes from non-determinism in the environment, not from assertion strength.

answer.text: Unit tests are actually the flakiest, so the top only looks flaky

feedback.text: Unit tests are the most stable; the top is genuinely the flakiest.

answer.text: Because the top layer runs most often

feedback.text: The top usually runs least often; flakiness is due to dependencies and timing, not frequency.

generalfeedback.text: Every additional integrated component, network hop, timing dependency, and piece of shared state adds a source of non-determinism, so end-to-end tests at the top flake most.

questiontext.text: When is adding more end-to-end tests genuinely justified despite their cost?

answer.text: For a few critical user journeys whose end-to-end confidence cannot be obtained adequately at a lower layer

feedback.text: Correct — E2E earns its place where only whole-system realism gives the needed confidence.

answer.text: Whenever a behaviour could also be covered by a unit test

feedback.text: If a unit test suffices, push down; do not duplicate it at E2E.

answer.text: To replace unit tests entirely for simplicity

feedback.text: Replacing the fast base with slow E2E tests inverts the pyramid.

answer.text: Never — E2E tests are never justified

feedback.text: A few E2E tests for critical flows are valuable; the point is to keep them few.

generalfeedback.text: Add E2E tests sparingly for critical end-to-end journeys where lower layers cannot give adequate confidence — not for behaviours a unit or integration test already covers.

questiontext.text: Which statement about the pyramid is a misconception?

answer.text: The narrow top means UI/E2E tests are unimportant

feedback.text: Correct — this is the misconception; the width reflects count/proportion and speed, not importance.

answer.text: The width of a layer reflects how many tests of that kind you should have

feedback.text: This is a correct reading of the pyramid, not a misconception.

answer.text: E2E tests are still needed, just kept few

feedback.text: This is correct — E2E tests remain valuable but are few.

answer.text: Lower layers give faster feedback than higher ones

feedback.text: This is a correct property of the pyramid, not a misconception.

generalfeedback.text: The pyramid is about test count/proportion and feedback speed, not importance. A thin top does not mean E2E tests are unimportant — only that few of them are needed.

questiontext.text: Because E2E tests are slow and flaky, a healthy pyramid should have zero end-to-end tests.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: A healthy pyramid keeps a few E2E tests for critical flows, not zero.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — the top is thin, not empty; a few E2E tests remain essential.

generalfeedback.text: The pyramid narrows to a few E2E tests, not none. Some end-to-end coverage is needed to confirm critical user journeys work through the whole system.

questiontext.text: A suite of 200 tests is currently inverted at 20 unit / 40 integration / 140 UI. You want to reach a 70% / 20% / 10% target while keeping the total at 200. How many unit tests must you add?

feedback.text: Correct — target unit = 70% of 200 = 140; you have 20, so add 140 − 20 = 120.
140 is the target unit count, but you already have 20, so you add only 120.
Recompute: target 140 minus current 20 is 120, not 100.
20 is the current unit count, not the number to add.

generalfeedback.text: Target unit = 0.70 × 200 = 140. Currently 20, so add 140 − 20 = 120. (Integration is already 40 = 20%; UI must drop from 140 to 20.)

questiontext.text: A suite of 100 tests is currently 40 unit / 10 integration / 50 UI. You want to reach a 70% / 20% / 10% target while keeping the total at 100. How many UI tests must you remove?

feedback.text: Correct — target UI = 10% of 100 = 10; you have 50, so remove 50 − 10 = 40.
10 is the target UI count, not the number to remove; you must remove 50 − 10 = 40.
50 is the current UI count; you keep 10, so remove only 40.
Recompute: 50 current minus 10 target is 40, not 30.

generalfeedback.text: Target UI = 0.10 × 100 = 10. Currently 50, so remove 50 − 10 = 40. (Unit rises from 40 to 70; integration rises from 10 to 20.)

name.text: Why not push everything to unit

questiontext.text: If unit tests are the fastest and cheapest, why not push every test down to the unit layer and drop the higher layers?

answer.text: Unit tests cannot catch faults in how components interact or in real end-to-end user flows; some confidence comes only from higher layers

feedback.text: Correct — interface and whole-system faults need integration and E2E tests.

answer.text: Because unit tests are actually the slowest layer

feedback.text: Unit tests are the fastest; the reason is coverage, not speed.

answer.text: Because higher layers are cheaper than unit tests

feedback.text: Higher layers are more expensive, not cheaper.

answer.text: You should, in fact, drop all higher layers

feedback.text: Dropping the higher layers would miss interaction and end-to-end faults entirely.

generalfeedback.text: Each layer catches faults the others cannot: unit tests miss interface/interaction faults and real user-flow problems, so integration and a few E2E tests remain necessary. "Push down" means using the lowest adequate layer, not eliminating higher ones.

name.text: Interaction bug slips through with thin middle

questiontext.text: A team has fast unit tests and a handful of E2E tests but almost no service-level tests, and bugs in how two services exchange data keep reaching production. What is the diagnosis and fix?

answer.text: An hourglass with a starved middle; add integration/service tests to catch interaction faults early

feedback.text: Correct — the missing middle lets interaction faults slip past unit tests and only sometimes get caught by the few E2E tests.

answer.text: An ice-cream cone; delete the unit tests

feedback.text: The unit base is fine; the problem is the missing integration middle, and you never delete the base.

answer.text: A healthy pyramid; no change needed

feedback.text: Interaction bugs reaching production show the integration layer is inadequate.

answer.text: Too many unit tests; remove some of them

feedback.text: Removing unit tests would not address the uncovered service interactions.

generalfeedback.text: Fast unit tests plus a few E2E tests but a starved middle is an hourglass. Interaction faults between services are best and fastest caught by integration/service tests, so grow that middle layer.

name.text: Lowest adequate level for an interaction fault

questiontext.text: A defect concerns how two services exchange data over their API. Applying "test at the lowest level that gives adequate confidence," which layer should own that test?

answer.text: Integration/service — it is the lowest layer that exercises the interaction between the two services

feedback.text: Correct — a unit test cannot see the interaction, and an E2E test is more than needed.

answer.text: Unit — it is the fastest layer

feedback.text: A unit test isolates one component and cannot exercise the cross-service interaction, so it does not give adequate confidence.

answer.text: UI/end-to-end — the most realistic layer

feedback.text: E2E would work but is slower and flakier than needed; the lowest adequate layer is integration.

answer.text: None — such faults cannot be tested

feedback.text: They are exactly what integration/service tests target.

generalfeedback.text: Push down to the lowest layer that still gives confidence. An interaction between two services is invisible to a unit test and overkill for E2E, so it belongs at the integration/service layer.

questiontext.text: The exact 70/20/10 split is a strict rule that every project must follow to have a valid pyramid.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: The specific numbers are illustrative, not a mandatory law.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — ratios like 70/20/10 are illustrative; the principle is the shape (wide base, thin top), not exact percentages.

generalfeedback.text: Concrete ratios are only rules of thumb to convey the shape. What matters is that unit tests dominate, integration tests are fewer, and UI/E2E tests are fewest — the exact numbers vary by project.
